אַל תַּשְׁחֵת is rendered 'Do not destroy' in both layers. Whether it is a tune name, a melody cue or a plea is open; I keep the plain sense and say so in the commentary. STEPBible lists it as a name; I glossed the two words separately.
The claim that the title belongs to 1 Samuel 19:11 rests on the title itself plus Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat David. Malbim's three-part division of the psalm is cited only as reported in the packet.
KJV numbers this title as verse 0 (the superscription), so the Hebrew verse 1 equals KJV 59:title; the verse map handles it. The Hebrew 59:2 is KJV 59:1.

agent_notes: 'uzzo' (his strength) does not agree with 'to you'. Verse 18 reads 'ozzi' (my strength), and many modern versions repair this verse to match; I have kept the Masoretic text as it stands, which the packet's five versions do not all do. Rashi and Radak take 'his' as the enemy's strength; Malbim reads it differently. I did not check manuscript or ancient-version evidence for the repair, so I make no claim about it. The choice is a judgment call.
Ketiv 'chasdo' (his loyalty) / Qere 'chasdi' (my loyalty). The packet gloss follows the Qere; both readings are explained in the note, citing Radak and Meiri.
'Hani'emo' (make them wander) is an imperative, not the passive that some English versions suggest; the KJV 'scatter' softens the nomadic 'wander about' (nua', as of Cain, Gen 4).

The syntax of the first clause is disputed. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Meiri read 'the sin of their mouth, the word of their lips' as the ground for the curse (let them be caught for it); YLT takes it as a statement. I kept it as an unattached accusative-like opening, which keeps the Hebrew ambiguity, and the dramatic layer follows the 'because of' reading shared by KJV, ASV, BBE. Meiri says the clause is elliptical or its order irregular.

Gloss for יְסַפֵּרוּ: STEPBible has '[which] they speak'. Piel of ספר is 'recount, tell'; I glossed 'they recount' because the verb is not the same as 'speak' (דבר) used for the lips. Radak and Metzudat David take it as others recounting the fate of the wicked, a reading I record but do not adopt.

The five English versions split between 'if not satisfied they grudge' (KJV, YLT) and 'tarry all night' (ASV, BBE). The literal layer keeps 'if not' and 'and they pass the night'; the dramatic layer chooses the hungry-night reading, which is Radak's.
